title: Roots and the system of stems

objectives.can: Name the stem of an Aramaic verb form: Peal, Pael, Haphel or Aphel, and their passive and reflexive partners.

explanation.summary: Almost every Aramaic verb is built on a root of three consonants, and the shape given to that root is called its stem. The stem tells you whether the verb is simple, doubled, causative, passive or reflexive. Learn to name the stem and you can read far more of Daniel and Ezra than the dictionary form of a verb would let you.

sections.heading: A root and a stem
body: A root is a set of three consonants that carries a core meaning. The root of the verb אֲמַר 'say' is the three consonants of that word, and the root of the verb קוּם 'stand, arise' is the three consonants of its headword. The root is not a word. It becomes a word when vowels, prefixes and sometimes a doubled consonant are added to it. That shaping is the stem.

The same root can be used in several stems, and the meaning changes with them. In this lesson the verb קוּם will be our guide, because the texts hold it in the simple stem (קָם 'he stood up'), in a causative stem (הֲקֵים 'he set up') and in a passive of the causative (הֳקִימַת 'it was made to stand'). The three consonants are the same each time; what differs is the stem.

sections.heading: The names of the stems
body: Aramaic grammar names the stems from the traditional model root, whose three consonants are pe, ayin and lamed. The simple stem is the Peal. The stem with a doubled middle consonant is the Pael. The causative is the Haphel, and in some verbs and some forms it is spelled with א instead of ה and called the Aphel. Each of these has a partner that is reflexive or passive: the Hithpeel and the Hithpaal, which begin with הִתְ-, and the passives Peil and Hophal, which change the vowels inside the word. A few verbs have a causative with שׁ, the Shaphel.

These names are Aramaic names. Hebrew has a different set of stems (it has a Niphal, which Aramaic lacks) and other patterns, and a Hebrew paradigm must not be carried over into Aramaic. The tables below come from the Aramaic of the Bible only.

The texts of the library label the conjugation of each verb form with a feature called HebForm. That name is borrowed from Hebrew, and its values are qatal, yiqtol, participle and so on. In this course we say perfect for qatal and imperfect for yiqtol, as Aramaic grammars do.

sections.heading: Marks to look for
body: Start from the front of the word. A prefix ה- (or הִתְ-, הָ-) or א- before the root points to a causative, a passive of the causative or a reflexive. A doubled middle consonant, shown by a dot in the letter, points to the Pael or the Hithpaal. A word with none of these is most often a Peal or a Peil.

In the imperfect and the participle the marks change, because those forms already have their own prefixes. The Haphel often keeps its ה after the prefix (יְהוֹדַע 'he will make known'), and the Aphel does not (יְקִים 'he will set up'). The participle of the Pael, the Haphel and the Aphel begins with מ- (מְהוֹדְעִין 'making known'), which the Peal participle lacks. These patterns are met again in A2.2 and A3.1.

A word of caution. A mark is a guide and not a proof. Weak roots lose consonants, so some forms look different from the pattern, and a few verbs are used in a stem whose usual meaning does not seem to fit. When the shape is unclear, find the headword and look at the neighbours of the form in its verse.

sections.heading: Stems and meaning
body: Do not give each stem one fixed meaning. The causative is the clearest case: הוֹדַע 'he made known' is the causative of יְדַע 'he knew'. But the Pael varies from verb to verb. בָּרִךְ 'he blessed' is a Pael of a root that in the Peal means 'kneel', and the relation between the two is not simple. Each verb must be learned in its stems.

The passive stems and the reflexive stems overlap: a Hithpeel form like הִשְׁתְּכַח can be translated 'was found', and it is a better guide to read it with its sentence than to decide the question from the prefix alone.

sections.heading: How common the stems are in the texts
body: The Aramaic of the Bible is small, and the stems are not equally common in it. The Peal has several hundred verb forms. The Haphel and the Pael have a hundred or so each at most, and the Aphel and the Hophal only a handful of forms. This is why this course spends most of its time on the Peal and then goes through the other stems one by one, using the verbs that really occur.

misunderstandings: Do not read the Hebrew stem names into Aramaic. The Aramaic word for the causative is Haphel or Aphel, and there is no Niphal. When a grammar of Hebrew gives a pattern, do not assume the Aramaic one looks the same.
A doubled consonant does not always mean the Pael. It can mark the Hithpaal, and some verbs double a consonant for other reasons. Check the prefix as well.
A prefix ה- is not always a causative marker. The same letter begins the reflexive Hithpeel and the passive Hophal. Read the whole word and its vowels.
The label HebForm is not a claim that Aramaic works as Hebrew does. It is a name taken from the data. Read qatal as the perfect and yiqtol as the imperfect.

deeper.heading: Why the causative has both ה and א
body: Grammarians have long observed that the older causative prefix was ה, and that א became the usual one in later Aramaic. Biblical Aramaic has both. Daniel and Ezra mostly have the Haphel, and the Aphel appears in a few verbs and forms. The data labels the verbs accordingly, and this course follows the labels of the analysed texts.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Nebuchadnezzar spoke and said: 'Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, who hath sent His angel, and delivered His servants that trusted in Him, and have changed the king's word, and have yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Five stems stand in this one verse. בְּרִיךְ (position 3) is a Peil participle, 'blessed'. שְׁלַח (11) is a Peal perfect, 'he sent'. וְשֵׁיזִב (13) is a Shaphel, 'and he delivered'. הִתְרְחִצוּ (16) is a Hithpeel, a form with the prefix הִתְ-. שַׁנִּיו (20) is a Pael, with the middle consonant doubled. Notice that the stem is a property of the word, whatever the meaning of the verb as a whole.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: גֲלִי (6) is a Peil perfect: the secret 'was revealed'. A passive stem lets the writer leave the revealer unnamed, as in many Aramaic sentences about God's action. בָּרִךְ (9) is a Pael perfect, 'blessed': Daniel is the subject. The stem tells you that the first verb is passive and the second is active.
